Floor ≥ 10% · buffer fully redeployed in three days, leverage 1.09×
No event contract since Aug 6 · JPUSD flat since Aug 5

reports.note: Best week of the year on the tape — +3.2%, led by NIQ and NU — and the per-name cap held under real temptation. But the 30.8% cash buffer earned by the SRPT exit was spent in three sessions, straight back into the same book, ending at 0.7% cash and 1.09× leverage. That is the familiar pattern: the win funds the size. Nothing is over the cap, yet there is no dry powder left and no room to be wrong twice.

buckets.name: Covered-call premium
buckets.note: The engine. Premium capture on held shares — managed, rolled, and bought back cheap.

buckets.name: Share legs
buckets.note: Where the damage clusters — a small number of oversized names, not the process.

buckets.name: Event contracts
buckets.note: High-volume churn near break-even; negative once costs are counted. Now wound down.

insights: Loss asymmetry is the leak: the average losing trade runs 1.7× the average winner, so a 60% win rate still nets out behind. Selection is fine — loss-sizing is the work.
The engine is real: covered-call premium wins 78% of its closes at a 3.7 profit factor. That edge is the business; everything else is management around it.

The event sleeve is now closed, not just shrinking — nothing traded since Aug 6. It was 91% of all closes for roughly no contribution, and retiring it removes the loudest source of noise in the record.
Share legs carry a 0.23 profit factor across just 33 closes — nearly all of it traceable to two names held past their stops. The per-name cap exists because of this line.
The honest trend: profit factor slipped from 0.92 to 0.88 and the payoff ratio from 0.61 to 0.59 this month. Marks recovered faster than the realized record did.

constraints.title: What this account may trade
permitted: Selling covered calls against held shares
constraints.note: Interactive Brokers currently limits this account to selling covered calls. Cash-secured puts — a core strategy in the principal's personal account and a preferred source of entry — are not permitted here. A mandate expansion is under review pending a business-plan revision.

p: The book is a concentrated set of retail-momentum equities wheeled with covered calls. After the SRPT exit freed roughly a third of the account, that cash was redeployed across nine names in a single week: the book now runs close to fully invested at about 1.09× gross, with the cash buffer down to under 1%. Single-name sizing stays inside the 20% cap, and the event-contract sleeve has been retired — nothing open.

ul: Covered-call premium on liquid small-cap momentum names — the engine of returns.
Cash treated as a position — currently spent, and rebuilding it is the open task.
Selective directional holds, sized small and governed by a written thesis.
The event-contract sleeve has been wound down; the book is equities and covered calls.
Single-name concentration capped at 20% of NAV — held this week at 18.6%.
Gross exposure about 1.09× NAV — modest margin in use, against a 10% cash floor now breached.
Broker mandate currently limits options activity to selling covered calls (see Approach).
Sizing, cash floor, and event exposure reviewed on a weekly discipline check.
Position size is the real risk lever — not the entry.
Define the risk before the entry, always.
Most of the tape is noise; the work is separating it from signal.

p: We trade a handful of durable ideas: asymmetry — small, defined risk for convex payoff; premium capture on names the crowd overpays to insure; and the humility that sizing, not selection, is where most books die.
Looking like a mad hatter today and being right over the long run is a feature, not a bug — provided the fundamentals underwrite the view.

The watchlist runs across financials, defense, technology, and petrochemicals. Themes of current interest: artificial intelligence, robotics, satellite communications, credit and insurance, and founder-led firms — along with several concepts kept off the page for brevity.

The largest threat to this book isn't the market — it's behavior. Conviction that becomes oversizing; a winner that invites a bigger bet; a loser held past its stop. We treat temperament as the primary risk to manage.

discipline.h: Rules that hold when discipline is hardest
ul: Max 20% of the book in any single name — conviction is expressed, not indulged.
A 10% cash floor at all times — dry powder is a position.
Hard stops, honored; no averaging down a losing thesis.
Every sizeable position carries a written thesis: catalyst, target, stop.

p: A single oversized position once gave back months of grinding. The position cap, the cash floor, and the stop discipline are scar tissue from lessons like that — codified so they never have to be re-learned the hard way.
The book is graded weekly on discipline, not only P&L — the Report Card is the enforcement mechanism. A green week with a broken rule still counts as a bad week.

story.h: Finding the signal in the noise
p: Pareidolia is the mind's tendency to see meaningful patterns — faces — in random noise. The idea began as a university capstone and was rebuilt for markets: read the world like an operator, keep the fundamentals in hand, and be willing to look like a mad hatter today if the long arc proves the read right.
Independent analysis. Independent taste. We form our own view, size it deliberately, and let a written framework — not the mood of the tape — govern the book.

Pareidolia was built from the ground up, on partner capital and no outside scaffolding. The intent was never to stay small — it is to compound a durable, inspectable process into something far larger, one disciplined decision at a time.
